questions.q: What should an entrepreneur's first goal be?
a: Creating meaning by improving customers' lives, not making money
Raising as much funding as possible before launch
Building a flashy brand that attracts attention
Hiring a large team as quickly as possible
questions.why: Lesson 1 says a company succeeds by making the world better, with money as a result rather than the aim.

questions.q: What does the summary say a money-first focus attracts?
a: Greedy, dishonest people who make customers uncomfortable
Investors who demand quick returns
Employees who value stability over risk
Competitors who copy your product
questions.why: Lesson 1 argues that greed as the main motive draws the wrong people and alienates customers.

questions.q: What are the three parts of the MAT framework?
a: Milestones, assumptions and tasks
Market, audience and timing
Mission, assets and team
Money, advertising and testing
questions.why: Lesson 2 introduces MAT as milestones, assumptions and tasks for early direction.

questions.q: What are assumptions in the MAT framework?
a: Beliefs about your idea that may be wrong and lack supporting data
Guaranteed facts confirmed by market research
The tasks you complete every week
The funding you expect to raise
questions.why: Lesson 2 says to list what you believe about your business that you have no data to support.

questions.q: Why is a business plan valuable even if investors never read it?
a: Writing it exposes gaps in your thinking and helps the team work together
It guarantees that your product will succeed
It replaces the need for a prototype
It legally protects your idea from rivals
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the process of writing a plan reveals blind spots and improves teamwork.
